title: Is using AI to help code things consider differently than using AI to create or art or story or text or something
author: katastatik
selftext:
So I'm in a unique position where I have a deep background in technology and music and can code, but I'm able to do things with Claude in minutes that would have taken me a week. 

But that's just me using it to reach very specific and very well thought through ideas that I have trying to do something. 

Is this viewed the same or differently than when people ask if people are using AI?

comments.author: Aromatic-Low-4578
comments.body: People generally don't care about AI generated code. It's the AI art that really seems to upset folks.

replies.author: Trashy_io
replies.body: What if my art is from generated code...

replies.author: stevbrisc
replies.body: we definitely care a ton if we're reviewing it..

replies.author: katastatik
replies.body: Yeah but if you were reviewing it it should be in the context of some sort of organization where there's an understanding that the people who are submitting this are using AI, right so that's just an understood annoyance. Here I'm talking about an independent person doing an independent thing that they're giving away. Not trying to make money just trying to show something that is a cool idea that was hard to create. That's a different story I think but yes I can imagine doing pull requests and code reviews with AI could be really tedious and irritating

I'm fairly new to vibecoding and I always some ideas for some small games. And thanks to AI, i shipped on [itch.io](http://itch.io) ( yep this is a big landmark for me  😄)  my first little HTML game this week .

All it tooks for me was 20 bucks for a sub to Claude and after 2 prompts I had a proof of concept running and I expanded from here. The GFX of my game is based on simple ascii forms. 

I tried to make some publicity on the releving subs and I was met with negative comments as soon as I mentionned AI. So yes , people care too much about AI and are gatekeeping their stuff like crazy.

replies.body:
I'm not sure why you got done voted out of existence here but...
People seem to overlook that anything you're doing with AI isn't doing anything without you trying to do something. It's very weird

replies.author: kazuyette
replies.body:
Don't worry for the downvotes, I'll survive 😉. 

This is only a little fun project for me to learn a bit about AI (agentic coding, .memory files , you name it ) instead of just treating it like a super search engine. 
My game is already on itch.io and I intend to get my little baby polished enough to publish it on Steam.
I will surely throw a 100 bucks away for the Steam fee but I don't care and who knows 😉 ?
I'm in for the fun and learn a bit in the process . If I ever win some money (even just 5 sales ) , I will be very happy to know that some people around the world are enjoying my game.


If I have faith , I'd love to release a mobile version of my game in the future.

replies.author: funkwizard4000
replies.body: Can you explain why you feel that way? What do you mean by ‘red flag’ specifically? I understand the term, but want to know your thoughts on why you apply it here.

replies.author: BloxxyVids
replies.body: I think it's a red flag because if a developer is primarily having the AI be the programmer, what will it mean for the future of the game? As complexity increases, AI will serve the purpose of accelerating updates but will no longer be able to be the primary programmer and maintainer, and it'll become extremely necessary that the developer understands the codebase at a deep level

replies.author: funkwizard4000
replies.body: So essentially you think that it is unrealistic to be able to trust the codebase to AI and that the game will eventually collapse under the weight of poor architectural decisions and coding practices from the AI. If AI was able to avoid these issues, or if the developer was able to use strict standards while still having AI generate the code, would you still consider it a red flag or problem?

replies.author: BloxxyVids

I think it would be quite lazy, but I also think that at that point, they shouldn't be doing traditional text based coding and should be using a game engine that simplifies stuff

but if the game is fun and the AI were to avoid the issues I don't think it should matter as much to the end user. 

from a developer standpoint, I think it's totally valid to be disapproving, but not as much from a user standpoint

replies.body:
You’re basically arguing the AI loses the memory to code effectively over time. Ithink the real problem is the dev loses the mental model of the code base and can’t prompt effectively anymore. 

I always argue that the dev needs to maintain the mental model. Just like architects have done for decades. Especially in large companies they rarely wrote the code themselves. Yet they understood it enough to talk to it and jump in if needed. 

Using AI is that. Lose the mental model the code goes to slop. Keep the mental model you still control it.

comments.author: AltusLudus
comments.body:
Disclaimer: I don't have anything against AI and am for it

But it's double standards, like writing really good code is an art form of itself, it should be the same standard for both as both have been trained on human generated content, be it art or code.

Some Artists are mad because AI is stealing (although not really) their jobs, and they use AI to code / automate their stuff in daily life, ask questions etc.

Some Developers are mad because AI is stealing their jobs and don't want to use AI to code. But generate memes, art assets for their game, use it in their daily life

I think we are scared as humans by this threat that we don't understand, but in reality it's just a really good algorithm and it'll cap out eventually, and humans will be using AI as an assistance in their daily work / life and we'll be all fine. Not saying a lot of shit won't happen, and some will suffer, but they'll figure it out, it's all going to be fine.

comments.author: Fail-Least
comments.body:
I definitely see a double standard.

For context, I have over 20 years of software engineering experience. I also earned advanced degrees from graduate programs researching AI and machine learning. At the same time, I took music lessons as a kid, played in a band through university, and I draw and paint as a hobby.

Both music and visual art came from my dad. He was not a professional musician or artist. They were just things he did to relax, and as a kid I thought that was incredibly cool.

So this is a long-winded way of saying: I chose software engineering as my profession, but I have always practiced art for the love of it.

That is why the conversation around AI-generated assets annoys me so much. People make a huge fuss about protecting “art” from AI, while casually minimizing the talent, creativity, research, engineering, and persistence that made AI possible in the first place.

Software engineering is treated like mere technical labor, as if it is not creative, as if building systems does not require taste, judgment, abstraction, and imagination. But somehow, once the output looks like an image, a song, or a story, suddenly everyone remembers that human creativity matters.

That is the double standard.

I care about art. I care about artists. But I am not going to pretend that the only creativity worth defending is the kind people already know how to romanticize. AI did not appear out of nowhere. It was built by human beings applying a different kind of talent, and that talent deserves respect too.

And whether people like it or not, AI is not going anywhere. It has a place in software engineering, and it has a place in creative work. The important question is not whether it should exist, but how we use it responsibly, honestly, and without pretending that one form of human creativity is sacred while another is disposable.

replies.author: SinchronousElectrics
replies.body: I think it’s because people see code as a means to an end and not as an art itself. Like if code works decently enough, the end user won’t ever notice any cool software constructs. But the fact that proper coding practices are woven in makes it so the project can scale in terms of size and scope effectively.

replies.author: katastatik
replies.body: I've made plenty of things before AI existed. I actually feel like I'm at the right point to be able to have a very clear complex vision and have a coding partner at this point that can actually make it happen. That is very rare in my experience

comments.author: OnDotZet
comments.body:
Yes. Digital art and creative stories are meant to convey creativity and a deep personal message. While proograms are meant to run a list of instructions to the letter as long as the code is correct in syntax and there are no errors

Meaning, art and writing in general care less about functionality and more about creativity. The opposite is true for code. As long as your code runs smoothly and works as you intend it to then there's nothing wrong with that. I'm not advocating AI btw, I think that using AI will limit your coding and creative capabilities, but if you use it for prototyping then that's perfectly fine, as long as you fix the bugs or bottlenecks in your code

replies.author: katastatik
replies.body:
I've been creating things my whole life. A couple of years ago at age 57 I released my first video game. No way I was involved in it won an international award for gameplay innovation. I don't even like games

The point that I'm trying to make is that I feel with my background, skills and experience, this is exactly the right time for me to be doing what I'm doing: I can code, but coding is not my calling. It is just a means to an end and having an entity to work with who is much better at coding than I am allows me to focus on what I'm good at. The ideas that make the whole thing happen.

The way that I'm using AI here for the work that I've presented is literally I describe something in significant detail that I'm trying to do and I go back and forth on Claude  with it until I get it where I want it to be. 

I think people think you write a paragraph long prompt and then sit back and it's doneYou write a paragraph long prompt and then sit back and wait and that's not at all how it works. I have literally hundreds of pages of back and forth iterative conversations about the work that I've done here.

Anyway I was just curious what you guys thought because I think there is a distinction but I don't know if everyone makes it

comments.author: soulfir
comments.body: The distinction people are drawing, even when they don't say it cleanly, is authorship versus assistance. Using AI to get from a precise idea in your head to working code faster reads as assistance, because the intent and the judgment are still yours and the output is verifiable, it runs or it doesn't. Generated art and prose hit different because there's often no correct target, so the tool isn't compressing your intent, it's supplying it. That's the actual line. The same tool feels fine when it executes your decision and feels hollow when it makes the decision for you. Worth being honest with yourself about which one you're doing in a given moment, because most projects are a mix of both.
